title: Stage 2: Reading data
summary: Give the API a list of tasks and serve them: the whole collection, and one task by id.

steps.title: Resources and GET
body: A REST API is organised around **resources**: the things your service knows about. Ours has one kind of resource, the task.
Two rules do most of the work:
- **The URL names the thing.** `/tasks` is the whole collection. `/tasks/2` is the single task whose id is 2. URLs are nouns.
- **The HTTP method says what to do with it.** `GET` means *show me*. Later stages add `POST` (create), `PUT` (replace) and `DELETE` (remove).
So you never write a URL like `/getTask?id=2`. The verb is already in the request: `GET /tasks/2`.

`GET` is a **safe** method: it only reads. A client, a browser or a cache may repeat a GET as often as it likes, and nothing on the server may change because of it. Keep that promise in every GET endpoint you write.
## Where the data lives

For now the tasks live in a `List<TaskItem>` in memory. It is created when the program starts and is lost when it stops. That is enough to learn every HTTP idea in this project. A real service would put a database behind the same endpoints.
```csharp
var tasks = new List<TaskItem>
new(1, "Learn C#", true),
app.MapGet("/tasks", () => tasks);
app.Run();
record TaskItem(int Id, string Title, bool Done);
Returning a list sends a JSON array. Each record in it becomes a JSON object.

steps.prompt: A client wants the task with id 7. Which request follows the REST conventions?
steps.explain: The URL names the resource (`/tasks/7`, task 7 inside the tasks collection) and the method carries the verb. `POST` is for creating, and it is not safe to repeat, so it is the wrong tool for reading.

static class DojoTests
public static async Task Run(HttpClient http)
await Dojo.TryAsync("The endpoints from stage 1 could be checked", async () =>
Dojo.Eq("GET /health still returns ok", "ok", await DojoWeb.Text(await http.GetAsync("/health")));
Dojo.Eq("GET / still names the service", "Tasks API", DojoWeb.Prop(await DojoWeb.Json(await http.GetAsync("/")), "name"));
await Dojo.TryAsync("GET /tasks could be checked", async () =>
var r = await http.GetAsync("/tasks");
DojoWeb.Status("GET /tasks responds 200 OK", 200, r);
Dojo.Check("GET /tasks responds with JSON", r.Content.Headers.ContentType?.MediaType == "application/json", "the content type was " + r.Content.Headers.ContentType);
var text = await DojoWeb.Text(r);
var json = await DojoWeb.Json(r);
Dojo.Check("GET /tasks returns a JSON array", json.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array, "the body was: " + text);
Dojo.Eq("the array holds tasks 1, 2 and 3 in that order", "1,2,3", Ids(json));
Dojo.Eq("task 1 has the title \"Learn C#\"", "Learn C#", DojoWeb.Prop(At(json, 0), "title"));
Dojo.Eq("task 1 is done", "true", DojoWeb.Prop(At(json, 0), "done"));
Dojo.Eq("task 2 has the title \"Build an API\"", "Build an API", DojoWeb.Prop(At(json, 1), "title"));
Dojo.Eq("task 2 is not done", "false", DojoWeb.Prop(At(json, 1), "done"));
Dojo.Eq("task 3 has the title \"Ship it\"", "Ship it", DojoWeb.Prop(At(json, 2), "title"));
Dojo.Check("property names are camelCase: id, title, done", text.Contains("\"id\"") && text.Contains("\"title\"") && text.Contains("\"done\""), "the body was: " + text);
// "1,2,3" for a JSON array of tasks, so one row can check which tasks came back and in what order.
static string Ids(JsonElement json) => json.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array
? string.Join(",", json.EnumerateArray().Select(e => DojoWeb.Prop(e, "id")))
: "(not a JSON array)";
static JsonElement At(JsonElement json, int index) =>
json.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array && index < json.GetArrayLength() ? json[index] : default;
static async Task<string> IdsOf(HttpClient http, string url) => Ids(await DojoWeb.Json(await http.GetAsync(url)));
static bool HasError(JsonElement json) => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(DojoWeb.Prop(json, "error"));
static Task<HttpResponseMessage> Patch(HttpClient http, string url, object body) =>
http.PatchAsync(url, JsonContent.Create(body));

steps.title: Route parameters
body: `/tasks/1`, `/tasks/2` and `/tasks/3` should not need three endpoints. Put a **route parameter** in braces and it matches any value in that position:
```csharp
app.MapGet("/users/{id}", (int id) => $"You asked for user {id}");
The name in the braces must match a parameter of the lambda. ASP.NET Core takes the text from the URL, converts it to the parameter's type, and passes it in. This is called **binding**.
## Route constraints
What if someone requests `/users/abc`? With plain `{id}` the route matches, the conversion to `int` fails, and the framework answers `400 Bad Request`.
Add a **constraint** and the route only matches when the value fits:
```csharp
app.MapGet("/users/{id:int}", (int id) => $"You asked for user {id}");

Now `/users/abc` does not match this route at all. If no other route matches either, the answer is `404 Not Found`, which is the honest one: there is no such resource. A constraint also lets `/users/{id:int}` and a later `/users/search` live side by side.

steps.prompt: Complete the endpoint so that `GET /orders/15` responds with `Order 15`, and `GET /orders/latest` does not match it.
steps.explain: The name in the braces must match the lambda parameter, and the constraint `:int` restricts the route to whole numbers, so `latest` is left for another route.

steps.title: Status codes and Results
body: Every HTTP response starts with a three-digit **status code**. The first digit is the category:
| Range | Meaning | Examples |
| 2xx | It worked | `200 OK` |
| 4xx | The client asked for something wrong | `400 Bad Request`, `404 Not Found` |
| 5xx | The server failed | `500 Internal Server Error` |
Clients read the code before they look at the body, so it has to tell the truth. Sending `200 OK` with a body that says "not found" forces every client to parse text to find out what happened.
When you return a plain object, ASP.NET Core sends `200 OK`. To choose the code yourself, return one of the `Results` helpers:
```csharp
app.MapGet("/users/{id:int}", (int id) =>
var user = users.FirstOrDefault(u => u.Id == id);
return user is null ? Results.NotFound() : Results.Ok(user);

`Results.Ok(user)` is 200 with the user as JSON. `Results.NotFound()` is 404 with no body. Both are of type `IResult`, which is why one lambda may return either: a lambda needs a single return type, and `user` and "nothing" do not share one.

steps.prompt: This is the lookup your endpoint will do, as a console program. What does it print?
code: record TaskItem(int Id, string Title, bool Done);
steps.explain: `FirstOrDefault` returns the first match, or `null` for a record type when nothing matches. That `null` is exactly the case that should become `404 Not Found`.

steps.prompt: Which family of status code fits each situation?
items: The request body is not valid JSON
steps.explain: Ask who has to change something for the request to succeed. If the client must fix the request, it is a 4xx. If the request was fine and your code broke, it is a 5xx.

steps.prompt: The only routes are the two below. What does `GET /tasks/abc` respond with?
steps.explain: `abc` fails the `:int` constraint, so the second route does not match, and neither does the first. No route means 404. Without the constraint the route would match and the failed conversion would give 400.

steps.title: One task by id
prompt: Add `GET /tasks/{id}` to fetch a single task.
- When a task with that id exists, respond `200 OK` with the task as a JSON object (not an array).
- When it does not, respond `404 Not Found`.
- Constrain the id to an integer, so that `GET /tasks/abc` is also `404 Not Found`.
`GET /tasks` must keep returning the whole list.
starter: record TaskItem(int Id, string Title, bool Done);
solution: return task is null ? Results.NotFound() : Results.Ok(task);
record TaskItem(int Id, string Title, bool Done);

Both branches must return an `IResult`: `Results.Ok(task)` when you found one, `Results.NotFound()` when `FirstOrDefault` gave you `null`.
